extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and researchers studying first-order logic and model theory
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, proofs, and constructions of fundamental meta-theorems of first-order logic (soundness, completeness, compactness, enumerability) together with Henkin-style model constructions and consequences for finite models and decidability.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOUNDNESS THEOREM
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that deductions lead only to 'correct' conclusions; proof idea: logical axioms are logically implied by anything, and modus ponens preserves logical implication. Proof proceeds by induction on a deduction: cases for logical axioms, premises, and modus ponens. See also Lemma 25A (every logical axiom is valid).

rubrics_metrics.name: LEMMA 25A — Every logical axiom is valid
rubrics_metrics.description: Every logical axiom (from the chosen axiom groups) is valid (logically implied by any structure/assignment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof inspects axiom groups (1–6) in order of complexity, using exercises referenced for some groups. Group 6 uses term/variable-replacement arguments; group 2 (quantifier axioms) relies on the substitution lemma. The lemma is the core semantic justification for soundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution Lemma (including Lemma 25B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the term t is substitutable for the variable x in the wff ϕ, then |=_A ϕ_x^t [s] iff |=_A ϕ [s(x | s(t))]. (Lemma 25B: for terms u, s(u_x^t) = s(x | s(t))(u).)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that substitution may be carried out either inside the formula/term or in the assignment with equivalent results. Proofs proceed by induction on terms (Lemma 25B) and on formulas (Substitution Lemma). Used to justify quantifier axiom validity (e.g., ∀x Px → P t). Attention to the precise 'substitutable' condition and alphabetic variants is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: COMPLETENESS THEOREM (GÖDEL, 1930)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If (Γ) |= ϕ, then (Γ) ⊢ ϕ. (b) Any consistent set of formulas is satisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts (a) and (b) are equivalent; proof given for countable languages via a Henkin-style construction: expand the language with countably many new constants, add Henkin sentences ¬∀xϕ → ¬ϕ_x^c to guarantee witnesses, extend to a maximal consistent (deductively closed) set, build a term model A with universe = set of terms and interpret predicates/functions by membership in the maximal set, then if equality present take quotient by the congruence E_A to get a model. Sketch highlights steps 1–6 and notes adjustments for uncountable languages (indexing by ordinals, Zorn's lemma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Henkin construction / steps for completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure to build a model from a consistent set Γ: (1) expand language with new constants; (2) for each formula ϕ and variable x add a formula ¬∀xϕ → ¬ϕ_x^c using fresh constant c, preserving consistency; (3) extend to a maximal consistent set Δ (deductively closed); (4) form structure A with domain = terms, interpret predicates/functions so Pt1...tn ∈ Δ iff (t1,...,tn) ∈ P^A; (5) show E^A (interpreting equality) is a congruence and form quotient A/E; (6) restrict back to original language to obtain desired model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details include choice of fresh constants avoiding earlier occurrences, using compactness/finite-deduction arguments to preserve consistency when adding Henkin sentences, proving |=_A ϕ*[s] iff ϕ ∈ Δ by induction on formula complexity, and handling equality via equivalence classes and homomorphism theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal consistent set (properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set Δ extending Γ is maximal consistent if (i) Γ ⊆ Δ, (ii) Δ is consistent and for any formula α either α ∈ Δ or (¬α) ∈ Δ, and (iii) Δ is deductively closed (if Δ ⊢ ϕ then ϕ ∈ Δ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction methods: use enumeration + compactness/truth-assignment argument or Zorn's lemma for larger languages. Maximality implies deductive closure and consistency prevents both α and ¬α being present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling equality by quotient construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When equality is in the language, interpret '=' in the preliminary term-structure A by a predicate E and then form the quotient structure A/E, where E_A = {(u,t) | u = t ∈ Δ}. The quotient collapses E-equivalent terms to ensure equality is interpreted as identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show E_A is an equivalence relation and a congruence (compatibility with predicates and functions), define A/E with universe of equivalence classes, interpret predicates/functions naturally, and use the natural homomorphism h to transfer satisfaction from A to A/E, obtaining a structure in which original equalities are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: COROLLARY 25C — Logical equivalence from provable biconditional
rubrics_metrics.description: If ⊢ (ϕ ↔ ψ), then ϕ and ψ are logically equivalent (i.e., |= (ϕ ↔ ψ)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from soundness: provable biconditional implies semantic equivalence in all structures/assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: COROLLARY 25D — Alphabetic variants are equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ' is an alphabetic variant of ϕ, then ϕ and ϕ' are logically equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses syntactic and semantic equivalence of renaming bound variables; applied in completeness proofs when changing to a variant where a term becomes substitutable.

rubrics_metrics.name: COROLLARY 25E — Satisfiable implies consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is satisfiable, then Γ is consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This corollary is equivalent to soundness; demonstration: a satisfiable set cannot yield a deduction of both ϕ and ¬ϕ because that would contradict the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: COMPACTNESS THEOREM
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If Γ |= ϕ, then for some finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ we have Γ0 |= ϕ. (b) If every finite subset Γ0 of Γ is satisfiable, then Γ is satisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs derive from completeness and finiteness of deductions: semantic entailment implies provability, which uses only finitely many premises; conversely, satisfiability of every finite subset implies consistency of whole set, hence completeness gives a model. The compactness theorem can be used constructively (e.g., via ultrapowers or Henkin methods) and underlies many model-theoretic arguments (e.g., obtaining infinite models from arbitrarily large finite ones).

rubrics_metrics.name: ENUMERABILITY THEOREM
rubrics_metrics.description: For a reasonable language, the set of valid wffs can be effectively enumerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable language: parameters effectively enumerable and the arity relations for predicate/function symbols decidable. Proof idea: the set of logical axioms (Λ) and hence deductions is decidable; enumerate all finite sequences and check which are deductions, listing the final formulas. Alternative: decide membership in axiom groups and then enumerate tautological consequences of Λ.

rubrics_metrics.name: COROLLARY 25F — Enumerability of theorems implied by a decidable Γ
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is a decidable set of formulas in a reasonable language, then (a) the set of theorems of Γ is effectively enumerable, and (b) the set {ϕ | Γ |= ϕ} is effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs: enumerate validities and filter those of the form αn → ... → α0 whose antecedents are in Γ; or note Γ ∪ Λ is decidable so its tautological consequences are enumerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: COROLLARY 25G — Decidability when Γ is complete and decidable
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume Γ is decidable and for any sentence σ either Γ |= σ or Γ |= ¬σ. Then the set of sentences implied by Γ is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Γ is inconsistent then trivial. Otherwise enumerate theorems until either σ or ¬σ appears, deciding entailment. Note caveat: we may not effectively know which branch (consistent/inconsistent) applies from a finite description of Γ.

rubrics_metrics.name: THEOREM 26A — Infinite model from arbitrarily large finite models
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set Σ of sentences has arbitrarily large finite models, then it has an infinite model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct sentences λ_k saying 'there are at least k things' and consider Σ ∪ {λ2, λ3, ...}. Every finite subset has a model by hypothesis, so by compactness the whole set has a model, which must be infinite. This pattern (describe desired properties by sentences, show finite consistency, apply compactness) is a standard method.

rubrics_metrics.name: COROLLARY 26B — Classes of finite/infinite structures not EC
rubrics_metrics.description: The class of all finite structures (for a fixed language) is not an elementary class (not Mod τ for any τ). The class of all infinite structures is not EC either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Theorem 26A: if Mod τ were exactly finite structures then its complement (infinite structures) would be elementary, contradicting the theorem. The class of infinite structures is EC (axiomatizable by {λ2,λ3,...}) but not elementary in the complement sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observations on finite structures and decidability (1–5) / THEOREM 26C
rubrics_metrics.description: Key observations: (1) any finite structure A is isomorphic to {1,...,n}; (2) a finite structure in a finite language can be finitely specified as a string; (3) given A, a wff ϕ, and an assignment of universe elements to free variables, one can effectively decide |=_A ϕ [s]; (4) given a sentence σ and n, one can decide whether σ has an n-element model; (5) the spectrum {n | σ has model of size n} is decidable. THEOREM 26C: For a finite structure A in a finite language, Th(A) is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs for Th(A) decidable: (i) reduce to universe {1,..,n} and evaluate sentences effectively; (ii) produce a sentence δ_A that axiomatizes A up to isomorphism and apply corollary 25G (completeness of theories of finite models). Observation (4) uses enumeration of all structures on {1,..,n} and checking satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: THEOREM 26D — Sentences with finite models effectively enumerable
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite language, the set {σ | σ has a finite model} is effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semidecision procedure: for given σ, systematically check n = 1,2,3,... whether σ has an n-element model (decidable for each n); if some n works, output σ. This enumerates all sentences having finite models.

rubrics_metrics.name: COROLLARY 26E — Complement of sentences true in every finite structure is enumerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Let FinTh be the set of sentences true in every finite structure. Then its complement (sentences not true in all finite structures) is effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: σ ∉ FinTh iff ¬σ has a finite model; apply the semidecision procedure from Theorem 26D to ¬σ to enumerate such σ.
